area: Area III. Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can pick the right runway and pattern for the conditions, enter, fly and leave a traffic pattern at towered and non-towered airports, and hold pattern altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots while keeping track of other traffic.
why: Most mid-air collisions happen in or near the traffic pattern, close to the ground [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. A standard, predictable pattern lets every pilot know where to look for everyone else.

prereading.what: The rectangular pattern, each leg, non-towered entries, and mid-air collision facts.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 8, 8-1 to 8-7

prereading.what: Recommended standard traffic pattern: entry, base turn, crosswind turn, departure, right-of-way.
prereading.label: AC 90-66C para 11

prereading.what: Pattern diagrams, entry from the upwind side, and pattern altitudes.
prereading.label: AC 90-66C Appendix A

prereading.what: Towered airports, leg names, pattern altitudes, right traffic (RP), segmented circle.
prereading.label: AIM 4-3-1 to 4-3-4

prereading.what: Wind indicators, segmented circle, and the key to pattern operations.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 14, 14-20 to 14-21

warmup: You are 10 miles from an airport with no tower, and nobody is talking on the radio. How will you decide which runway to use and which way to turn?

key_terms.def: The set path around a runway for arriving and departing airplanes: its direction, altitude, and how you enter and leave it [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].
The altitude you fly the pattern at. Usually 1,000 feet above the airport for propeller airplanes unless the Chart Supplement says otherwise [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]].
Flown parallel to the landing runway, opposite the landing direction [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]].
At right angles to the runway off its approach end, from downwind to the extended centerline [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]].
The path that continues straight ahead along the extended runway centerline after the departure leg. ATC uses it for separation, spacing or sequencing [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c2]].
Common Traffic Advisory Frequency: the frequency used for advisories at an airport without an operating tower. It may be UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS, or tower frequency [[1:336|PHAK 14-2]].
A ground marker system that shows wind, landing direction, runway alignment and pattern direction [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].
Automated weather stations giving minute-by-minute observations, often broadcast on a VHF frequency [[34:88|AIM 7-1-10]].
A pair of counter-rotating vortices trailing from the wingtips of every aircraft in flight [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]].
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

chunks.title: The pattern: legs, entry and exit

body.p: Every pattern is a rectangle around the runway. Learn the leg names; you will use them on every radio call [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]].

head: Leg
What it is
rows: Departure
Straight ahead after takeoff along the extended centerline, until at least 1/2 mile past the runway end and within 300 feet of pattern altitude [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]]
Crosswind
At right angles to the runway, off its takeoff end [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]]
Downwind
Parallel to the runway, opposite the landing direction. About 1/2 to 1 mile out [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Base
At right angles to the runway, off the approach end [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]]
Final
Along the extended centerline, in the landing direction, down to the runway [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2]]
Upwind

Straight ahead along the extended centerline after departure; an extension of the departure leg that ATC uses for separation, spacing or sequencing [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c2]]. On a go-around, turn slightly to the side so you can see departing traffic [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]

bullets: All turns are to the left unless the airport shows they should be to the right [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].
Pattern altitude for propeller airplanes: 1,000 feet AGL, unless the Chart Supplement publishes another one [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]].

callout.text: Everyone at the same altitude = everyone easier to see. A common altitude is the key factor in cutting collision risk at non-towered airports [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

body.p: Non-towered patterns are always entered at pattern altitude [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Descending entries create collision hazards and should be avoided [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

bullets: From the downwind side: fly a 45° entry to downwind, aimed at a point abeam the runway midpoint [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
Why 45°? If traffic blocks you, you can turn away, fly clear and try again, all while scanning [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

body.p: Arriving from the upwind side (the side away from downwind):

head: Method
How
rows: A. Preferred

Announce. Cross midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude (normally 1,500 feet AGL; 2,000 feet AGL if large or turbine airplanes use the airport). About 2 miles clear, scan, descend to pattern altitude, then turn to enter at 45° to downwind at midfield [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
B. Alternate
Enter on a midfield crosswind at pattern altitude, scan, announce, then turn downwind. Don't use it if the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]

body.p: Either way, give way to airplanes on the 45° entry and on downwind [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].
Leaving the pattern [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6-11.8]]:

bullets: After takeoff or a go-around, continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end of the runway.
Staying in the pattern: turn crosswind beyond the departure end and within 300 feet below pattern altitude. Turn downwind at pattern altitude.
Departing: go straight out, or turn 45° (left for left traffic, right for right traffic) beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude.

callout.text: Straight-in approaches are discouraged at non-towered airports. If you fly one, announce 8 to about 10 miles out. You get no priority over airplanes in the pattern [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

check.q: You arrive from the side opposite downwind at a non-towered airport with a 1,000-foot AGL pattern. At what height do you cross midfield using the preferred method?
check.a: At least 500 feet above pattern altitude, normally 1,500 feet AGL [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

body.p: At a towered airport, ATC tells you how to enter and gives a clearance to land. At a non-towered airport, you pick the pattern yourself, follow the rules, and talk on the CTAF [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

head: Towered (operating tower)
Non-towered
rows: Radio

Two-way radio required. In Class D, before entering the airspace [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)]]. At a towered airport in Class E or G: before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]]
Not required, but announce your intentions on the CTAF [[1:336|PHAK 14-2]]
Entry
Tower may have you enter at any point or fly straight in [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]
Normally a 45° entry to downwind at midfield, at pattern altitude [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Turns
Circle to the left unless told otherwise [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(f)]]
Left turns unless light signals or markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]
Landing
Need a clearance to take off, land, or use a runway or taxiway [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]
No clearance. You see and avoid [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]]
First call
About 15 miles out [[33:237|AIM 4-3-2]]

callout.text: 91.126 (Class G) sets the turn direction. 91.127 makes 91.126 apply in Class E. 91.129 (Class D) adds two-way radio and clearances, and says you must also follow 91.126 and 91.127 [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.129(a)]].

body.p: The FAA regulates pattern flow (turn direction), not how you enter [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]]. Entry methods come from the AIM, the AFH and AC 90-66C.
Non-towered radio calls [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9]]:

bullets: Departing: before taxiing, and before taxiing onto the runway.
Arriving: 10 miles out; entering downwind, base and final; leaving the runway.
UNICOM CTAFs include 122.7, 122.8, 122.725, 122.975 or 123.0. No tower, FSS or UNICOM: MULTICOM 122.9.

body.p: Say the airport name at the start and end of each call. Say the runway number, not "active runway" [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]]. Position calls: "entering left downwind runway [XX]," "on left base runway [XX]," "on final runway [XX]" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Use the airport name as charted, e.g. "Midwest National traffic" [[17:12|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

callout.text: Never say "any traffic in the area, please advise." It is not a recognized phrase [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.8.1]]. Don't announce your sequence ("number 3"), either; that is ATC's job [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

body.p: A part-time tower that is closed is a non-towered airport: use the CTAF and self-announce [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].

check.q: You are inbound to a Class D airport. When must you have two-way radio contact?
check.a: Before entering the Class D airspace, and keep it while inside [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]].

body.p: Land and take off on the runway most nearly aligned into the wind [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]]. If other airplanes are already in the pattern, use the same runway they are using [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].
Get the wind before you arrive:

head: Source
What you get
rows: ATIS (towered airports)
Recorded weather, runways in use and other information. Normally updated once per hour, each update with a new letter code [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]]
ASOS/AWOS
One-minute weather, usually receivable within about 25 NM of the airport below 10,000 feet. The frequency is on sectionals and in the Chart Supplement [[33:274|AIM 4-3-27]]
UNICOM
On request: weather, wind, recommended runway. Operators don't have to answer and there are no standards for what they say [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.3]]
Chart Supplement
Pattern altitude, right traffic, how to operate pilot-controlled lighting [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]] [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.1]] [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3]]

callout.text: Winds in ATIS and ASOS/AWOS broadcasts are magnetic [[34:89|AIM 7-1-10]], and so are runway numbers [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]]. Wind 270 favors Runway 27 with no math.

body.p: No radio info? Look at the ground. Check wind indicators even if someone gave you wind on the CTAF, because that information may not be accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. Check them from well above pattern altitude, then fly well clear before descending to enter [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]].

bullets: Wind sock/cone: the large end points into the wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].
Tetrahedron: the small end points in the direction of landing. In light or calm winds it may not match the calm-wind runway [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].
Traffic pattern indicators: L-shapes at each runway end. The short leg of the L shows which way you turn [[24:166|AFH 8-2]].
Trick: mentally enlarge the indicator for your runway, and your base and final legs appear [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].

body.p: Right traffic shows on sectional charts as "RP" plus the runway, e.g. RP 32. No RP means left traffic [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]]. "*RP" means special conditions; check the Chart Supplement [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3]].

check.q: The AWOS gives wind 330 at 12. The airport has Runways 3-21 and 14-32. Which runway do you choose?
check.a: Runway 32, the runway most nearly aligned into the wind [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]]. AWOS wind is magnetic, like runway numbers [[34:89|AIM 7-1-10]].

body.p: You need to find the runway, line up on the right one, and know where to stop. Key items for the pattern:

head: Item
What it tells you
rows: Runway number
Magnetic direction to the nearest 10° [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]]. Parallel runways add L, C or R [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]]
Displaced threshold
White arrows lead to a white bar. Less runway to land on. The part before the bar is available for takeoffs in either direction and for landings from the opposite direction [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]]
Yellow X
Runway or taxiway closed [[1:348|PHAK 14-14]]
Hold position marking
Two solid and two dashed yellow lines. At a non-towered airport, cross only when the runway is clear and no one is on final [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]]
Rotating beacon
Flashing white and green = civilian land airport [[1:350|PHAK 14-16]]
Runway edge lights

White. On instrument runways, yellow on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4b]]. Runway end lights show red toward the runway and green outward to landing aircraft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4c]]
Taxiway lights
Edge lights blue; centerline lights green [[1:353|PHAK 14-19]]
REIL
A pair of synchronized flashing lights at the threshold, for quick runway-end ID [[1:351|PHAK 14-17]]
VASI/PAPI

Visual glidepath; each light is white in the upper part of its beam and red in the lower part [[1:350|PHAK 14-16]]. PAPI (usually left side): 2 white + 2 red = on the 3° glide path; all white = high; all red = low [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2]]

body.p: Pilot-controlled lighting: tune the listed frequency and key the mic within 5 seconds: 7 times for highest, 5 for medium or lower, 3 for lowest intensity [[1:353|PHAK 14-19]]. The Chart Supplement tells you if the CTAF controls the lights [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.4]].

callout.text: Landing on a runway with a visual approach slope indicator in Class D: stay at or above the glide path until a lower altitude is needed for a safe landing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]].

body.p: At night, fly toward the beacon until you can pick out the runway lights. Identify the threshold and edge lights before setting up the pattern [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

check.q: On downwind you see a big yellow X on the runway you planned to use. What does it mean?
check.a: The runway is closed [[1:348|PHAK 14-14]]. Pick another runway, and check NOTAMs next time.

body.p: The right-of-way rules apply all through the pattern [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]]. Whatever the rules say, every pilot must see and avoid, and must not pass over, under or ahead of an aircraft with the right-of-way unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

head: Situation
Who has right-of-way / what to do
rows: Distress
The aircraft in distress, over everyone [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]
Converging, same category
The aircraft on the other's right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
Different categories

Balloon over all others; glider over powered aircraft; aircraft towing or refueling over other powered aircraft; airship over other powered aircraft except one towing or refueling [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
Head-on
Both alter course to the right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(e)]]
Overtaking
The one being overtaken. Pass well clear on the right [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]
Landing
Aircraft on final or landing, over aircraft in flight or on the surface [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]
Two aircraft landing
The lower one, but it can't cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]

body.p: A glider, including its tow plane while towing, has right-of-way over powered aircraft [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]]. A pilot flying a straight-in has no priority over pattern traffic [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].

callout.text: Even if you have the right-of-way, yield if the other airplane seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

check.q: You are on base at 700 feet AGL. Another airplane is on a long final at 500 feet AGL. Who goes first?
check.a: The airplane on final. It is lower and already on final, and you can't cut in front of it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

body.p: Here is a standard left pattern at a non-towered airport. Speeds, flaps and power come from your POH; the AFH gives generic guidance.

bullets: 1. Early: get ATIS or AWOS, set the CTAF, and look up pattern altitude and direction. Report 10 miles out [[24:170|AFH 8-6]] [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
2. Find the runway in use, then descend to pattern altitude well clear of the pattern [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]].
3. Enter on a 45° to downwind, abeam midfield, level at pattern altitude. Announce [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
4. Downwind: 1/2 to 1 mile out, parallel to the runway. Do the before-landing checks. Set power to fit traffic; typical piston singles fly 70 to 90 knots [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].
5. Abeam the approach end: reduce power and start descending [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
6. When the approach end is about 45° behind you, make a medium-bank turn to base. Announce [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.4]].
7. Base: crab to hold a track perpendicular to the runway. Target about 1.4 VSO; set flaps as recommended. Look for traffic on final before turning [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

8. Final: finish the turn at least 1/4 mile from the runway [[17:21|AC 90-66C App A]]. Line up on the centerline, confirm the runway number, and use the POH speed (1.3 VSO if none) [[24:174|AFH 9-3]] [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

9. Going around or staying in the pattern: climb straight ahead past the runway end, turn crosswind within 300 feet of pattern altitude, and level off at pattern altitude on downwind [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6-11.7]].

body.p: ACS tolerances and what the examiner watches:

head: Element
Standard
rows: Pattern altitude
±100 feet (ACS PA.III.B.S5)
Airspeed
Appropriate airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.III.B.S5)
Ground track
Correct for wind drift to keep the proper track (ACS PA.III.B.S3)
Orientation
Stay oriented to the runway in use (ACS PA.III.B.S4)
Spacing
Keep situational awareness and proper spacing from other aircraft (ACS PA.III.B.S6)
Procedures
Follow recommended pattern procedures (ACS PA.III.B.S2)

body.p: With a strong wind on final, put base closer to the runway than normal [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. In gusty air, pilots often add half the gust factor to approach speed: 70 knots with 15-knot gusts becomes about 77 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

check.q: Where on downwind do you start descending?
check.a: Hold pattern altitude until at least abeam the approach end of the landing runway, then reduce power and descend [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

body.p: The pattern is a rectangular course around a runway. The skills are the same: hold a set distance, altitude and airspeed, and angle into the wind to hold your track [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

head: Leg (landing into the wind)
Wind effect
Correction
rows: Departure/upwind
Headwind, slow groundspeed
Little or no crab [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
Crosswind
Wind from the side, pushing you toward the inside
Turn less than 90° and angle into the wind [[24:152|AFH 7-6]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
Downwind
Tailwind, fast groundspeed
Don't descend too much before base [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]; steeper bank in the turn to base [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
Base
Crosswind, often drifting you away from the runway
Angle into the wind so the track stays perpendicular to the centerline [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]
Final
Wind changes your glide distance over the ground
Adjust pitch and power for the wind [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]

body.p: Groundspeed changes in the turns, so bank changes too: steeper when groundspeed is high, shallower when it is low [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. The downwind-to-base turn starts with a relatively steep bank [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].

Staying oriented: keep the runway in sight and know where every leg is. Use the runway numbers and the heading indicator. At night, setting the heading bug to runway heading is an excellent reference for the legs [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

callout.text: Don't fix an overshoot of final with a steep turn. If you have to rush the turn, go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

check.q: Landing Runway 36 in left traffic, wind from 360. On which leg will the tailwind be strongest, and what does that do to your turn to base?
check.a: Downwind. Higher groundspeed brings base sooner and needs a steeper bank in the turn, so don't descend too much early [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

body.p: The NTSB says the most probable cause of mid-air collisions is a pilot failing to see and avoid [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Most reported mid-air collisions happen on final or short final [[24:171|AFH 8-7]].

bullets: Mid-airs mostly happen in daylight and good visibility [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
They are most likely between two aircraft going the same direction [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
Nearly all happen at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
Some aircraft have no radio, so silence doesn't mean the pattern is empty [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]].

body.p: Beat the blind spots. High wings block the view above, low wings block below; a low wing above a high wing is the worst case. Bank now and then to look, and check behind you [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Scan in short steps of no more than 10°, looking at least 1 second each [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Keep lights and strobes on [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.10]].
ADS-B In helps, but not every aircraft shows on it. Don't fixate on a tablet or the panel [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

Distractions and lost awareness: crowding, climbs and descents, and being busy in the cockpit all raise accident risk near airports [[33:237|AIM 4-3-1]]. Distractions start small and pull your eyes from scanning [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Manage the workload:

bullets: Listen to ATIS/AWOS and set frequencies before you get close [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Do checklists early so you can focus on traffic [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
If overloaded: stop, think, slow down, and prioritize. Fly the airplane first [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

body.p: Spacing: before joining downwind, adjust course or speed to fit in [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. You may vary the pattern size to fit your airplane [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]]. At a tower, shallow S-turns are OK, but never make a 360 in the pattern without telling the controller [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]]. If the turn to final would cause a conflict, go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

check.q: Your low-wing airplane is on downwind. Where is your blind spot, and how do you clear it?
check.a: Below you. Lower a wing now and then to look before turning, and check behind you [[24:169|AFH 8-5]] [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

chunks.title: Risk: wind shear and wake turbulence

body.p: Wind shear near the ground is especially dangerous because you have little height to recover [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: Headwind turning to tailwind: airspeed and performance drop. Tailwind turning to headwind: they rise [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Causes: fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions, and strong winds aloft (greater than 25 knots) [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

A microburst downdraft is typically less than 1 mile across, spreading out near the ground to about 2 1/2 miles. Downdrafts can reach 6,000 fpm and surface winds 45 knots (a 90-knot headwind-to-tailwind shear). It seldom lasts more than 15 minutes after it hits the ground, and its winds keep strengthening for the first 5 minutes [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]]. On approach it can force you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

A microburst is the most severe type of wind shear, and more than one can occur in the same storm [[28:263|AWH 22-8]] [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. If you reduce power and lower the nose for the first headwind gust, you are nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits; you can stall or land short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Be ready to go around at the first sign; at low altitude recovery may be impossible [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].
Larger airports may have LLWAS or similar systems. The tower relays alerts, e.g. "Wind shear alert, airport wind 230 at 8, south boundary wind 170 at 20" [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7]].
ATC issues wind shear/microburst alerts to all arriving and departing aircraft, and the ATIS keeps a statement for 20 minutes after the last report [[28:400|AWH 26-33]].

body.p: Wake turbulence: every aircraft makes it, so expect it in a pattern, especially behind other traffic [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]]. Vortices are strongest when the aircraft is heavy, slow and clean [[1:361|PHAK 14-27]]. They sink and, near the ground, drift sideways at 2–3 knots. A light quartering tailwind is the worst case [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

head: Following a larger aircraft
Do this
rows: Landing behind it, same runway
Stay at or above its final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Landing behind a departing aircraft
Land well before its rotation point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Taking off behind it
Rotate before its rotation point and climb above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
After its low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before taking off or landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]

callout.text: Avoid the area below and behind the aircraft making the wake, especially at low altitude [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]].

check.q: A business jet just did a touch-and-go on your runway in a light quartering tailwind. What do you do?
check.a: Wait at least 2 minutes before your takeoff or landing; the vortices may still be along the runway [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Descending into the pattern
Be level at pattern altitude before you enter [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]]
Short entry leg; joining without seeing the traffic
Fly a long enough 45° entry to see the whole pattern [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Not assessing the wind / no wind correction
Check the wind before entry and crab as needed on each leg [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Losing altitude or airspeed while busy
Trim, cross-check, and do checklists early [[24:153|AFH 7-7]] [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]
Descending too far on downwind with a tailwind
Keep enough height to continue the descent on base [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Overshooting final, then steepening the turn
Go around instead [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
Flying too fast or too slow for the traffic
Use the POH speeds and adjust power on downwind [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]
Lining up on the wrong runway or a taxiway
Check the runway number and alignment on every final [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Waiting too long to go around
Expect any approach may end in a go-around. Landing expectancy and pride delay it [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]

check.q: Why is pressing on with a bad approach so tempting?
check.a: Landing expectancy (believing it will work out) and pride (thinking a go-around means failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

f1.caption: Traffic pattern operations—single runway (AC 90-66C, Appendix A).
f1.alt: Green diagram of a left-hand rectangular pattern around a runway with numbered points: 1 the 45-degree entry to downwind, 2 downwind, base, 3 final, 4 departure, 5 crosswind turn, and 6 two ways to depart (straight out or a 45-degree turn). A segmented circle sits beside the runway.

scenario.title: Busy Saturday at a non-towered field
scenario.setup: You are flying solo to a non-towered airport with Runways 9-27. Twelve miles out, the AWOS gives wind 250 at 10 gusting 18. On the CTAF, a Cessna reports a left downwind for 27, a Bonanza says it is 6 miles east for a straight-in to 9, and a twin just did a touch-and-go on 27. You arrive from the south, the side opposite the left downwind for 27. While you set up, a passenger asks you about a warning light on the panel.

questions.q: Which runway do you plan for, and why?
questions.a: Runway 27. It is most nearly into the wind, and the traffic already in the pattern is using it [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]] [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].

questions.q: The Bonanza's straight-in to 9 will meet 27 traffic head-on. What do you do?
questions.a: Call the Bonanza on the CTAF and clarify its intentions [[17:12|AC 90-66C 10.1]]. A straight-in pilot has no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]]. Keep scanning toward the east.

questions.q: How do you enter from the south?
questions.a: Announce, cross midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude, fly about 2 miles clear, descend to pattern altitude, then turn to enter on a 45° to left downwind at midfield, giving way to the Cessna [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

questions.q: How do you handle the passenger's question about the warning light?
questions.a: Fly the airplane and scan first. Small distractions can pull your eyes inside. Stop, think, slow down and prioritize; if needed, leave the pattern to sort it out [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: What do the gusts and the twin's touch-and-go mean for your landing?
questions.a: Add about half the gust factor to approach speed, within POH limits [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Allow at least 2 minutes after the twin's touch-and-go, and stay above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

skills.do: Identify the runway in use, markings (numbers, thresholds, closed-runway Xs, hold lines), signs, the segmented circle, and airport lighting.
skills.practice: Before each flight, study the airport diagram and Chart Supplement. On every approach, name the runway, threshold type and lighting out loud.

skills.do: Enter, fly and leave the pattern using the recommended procedures and radio calls.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the pattern with radio calls. Practice 45° entries and the upwind-side entry at different airports with your CFI.

skills.do: Correct for wind drift so each leg's track stays square to the runway.
skills.practice: Fly rectangular courses in different winds, then pattern work on gusty or crosswind days with your CFI.

skills.do: Stay oriented to the runway in use, day and night, without losing sight of it.
skills.practice: Say each leg and the runway heading aloud. Set the heading bug to runway heading.

skills.do: Hold pattern altitude ±100 feet and appropriate airspeed ±10 knots.
skills.practice: Learn the power settings for downwind and descent in your airplane. Trim on every leg and cross-check altitude and airspeed.

skills.do: Keep track of other traffic and maintain proper spacing; extend, adjust or go around when needed.
skills.practice: Practice at busy airports. Build a mental picture from radio calls and confirm it by spotting each airplane.

quiz.q: Unless a different altitude is published, what is the recommended pattern altitude for a propeller airplane?
options: 500 feet AGL
800 feet AGL
1,000 feet AGL
1,500 feet AGL
quiz.why: Propeller-driven aircraft enter the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]].

quiz.q: At a non-towered airport in Class G airspace, which way must you turn when approaching to land?
options: Always left
Left, unless approved light signals or visual markings show right turns
Either way, at the pilot's choice
Whichever way the UNICOM operator says
quiz.why: Left unless the airport displays approved light signals or visual markings for right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

quiz.q: What is the normal way to enter the pattern at a non-towered airport from the downwind side?
options: Straight-in to final
Descending onto base
A 45° entry to downwind abeam midfield, at pattern altitude
Crossing over the runway end at pattern altitude
quiz.why: The normal entry is a 45° angle to downwind, toward a point abeam the runway midpoint [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

quiz.q: If you stay in the pattern after takeoff, when should you turn crosswind?
options: At 300 feet AGL
Beyond the departure end of the runway, within 300 feet of pattern altitude
As soon as you're past the midpoint of the runway
Only when reaching pattern altitude, over the runway
quiz.why: Turn beyond the departure end and within 300 feet below pattern altitude [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].

quiz.q: Two airplanes are approaching to land. Which has the right-of-way?
options: The faster one
The one at the higher altitude
The one at the lower altitude, as long as it doesn't cut in front of one on final
The one that called first on the CTAF
quiz.why: The lower aircraft has the right-of-way but can't cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

quiz.q: Where are most reported mid-air collisions in the pattern?
options: Crosswind leg
Downwind leg
Final and short final
Upwind leg
quiz.why: Most reported mid-air collisions occur on the final or short-final leg [[24:171|AFH 8-7]].

quiz.q: At an uncontrolled field with ASOS/AWOS, about how far out can you normally receive the broadcast?
options: 5 NM
10 NM
About 25 NM below 10,000 feet
50 NM at any altitude
quiz.why: The one-minute weather should be available within about 25 NM of the airport below 10,000 feet [[33:274|AIM 4-3-27]].

quiz.q: Landing behind a larger airplane on the same runway, what avoids its wake?
options: Stay below its approach path and land short of its touchdown point
Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point
Land at the same point it did
Fly a faster approach
quiz.why: Stay at or above the larger aircraft's final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

takeaways: Fly a standard rectangle at a common altitude, normally 1,000 feet AGL. Turn left unless marked otherwise.
At non-towered airports, enter on a 45° to midfield downwind, level at pattern altitude, and announce on the CTAF.
Choose the runway most nearly into the wind, or the one traffic is already using. Get the wind from ATIS/AWOS or the wind sock.
Hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, and crab on every leg to keep the track square.
Most mid-airs happen near the runway in good weather. Keep scanning, keep your lights on, and go around if spacing goes bad.
Stay above and behind a larger aircraft's flight path, and wait at least 2 minutes after its touch-and-go.
cfi_notes: Have students chair-fly the full pattern with radio calls before the first pattern lesson; workload is the main barrier.
Common student fault: rolling into downwind or base still descending from cruise. Insist on a level entry at pattern altitude.
Examiners often ask students to explain the upwind-side entry and why the FAA discourages straight-ins at non-towered airports (AC 90-66C).
Teach 'L-indicator: short leg = base' with the segmented circle on the ground; students mix up the tetrahedron and the wind sock.
Note: the PHAK gives 70–80 knots for fixed-gear singles on downwind (14-3); the AFH gives 70–90 knots for typical piston singles (8-5). Use the POH.
Students lose orientation on base at unfamiliar airports. Have them name the runway heading and the next leg's heading before each turn.

Source differences (lesson follows the AIM): the AFH (8-4) and AC 90-66C Appendix A describe the upwind leg as parallel to the runway in the landing direction; the current AIM 4-3-2c2 defines it as the straight-ahead extension of the departure leg. PHAK 14-18 calls the caution-zone edge lights amber; AIM 2-1-4b says yellow. PHAK 12-11 gives a microburst as 1-2 miles across lasting 5-15 minutes; AIM 7-1-24 says the downdraft is under 1 mile across (outflow to about 2 1/2 miles) and seldom lasts more than 15 minutes after reaching the ground. AWH 22-8 gives a typical microburst diameter under 2.5 miles and a lifespan of about 5-15 minutes.
gaps: Pattern speeds, power settings and flap use are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM. The AFH gives only generic guidance (1.4 VSO on base, 1.3 VSO on final).

AC 00-54 (Pilot Windshear Guide), cited by the PHAK, was cancelled by the FAA in 2022; this lesson uses the Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) instead. AWH 22-10 to 22-18 covers microburst effects, warning signs and the general principle of holding pitch attitude and accepting lower airspeed, but its encounter studies appear to involve large, crew-flown airplanes (crew coordination, stick shakers, aft body contact) and it gives no step-by-step windshear escape procedure for small airplanes. Get the airplane-specific technique from the POH/AFM and your CFI.

activities.title: Fly the arrival in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Get the AWOS, set the CTAF, and report 10 miles out
Find the runway in use, then descend to pattern altitude well clear
Enter on a 45° to midfield downwind, level, and announce
On downwind, do the before-landing checks
Abeam the approach end, reduce power and start down
With the runway end about 45° behind you, turn base and announce
On final, line up and confirm the runway number

activities.title: True or false: wake and wind shear

cards.s: Wake vortices are strongest behind an airplane that is heavy, slow and clean (flaps and gear up).
cards.why: Yes. Flaps and gear speed up wake decay, so heavy, clean and slow makes the strongest vortices [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]].

cards.s: Landing behind a larger airplane on the same runway, touch down before its touchdown point.
cards.why: No. Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: After a larger airplane's touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes before you take off or land.
cards.why: Yes. Vortices settle and drift near the ground and may still be along the runway [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: Near the ground, a light quartering tailwind is the worst case for wake turbulence.
cards.why: Yes. It can leave vortices along much of the final approach and extended centerline, not just in the touchdown zone [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

cards.s: A sudden jump in airspeed on final near a storm is a good time to pull power and lower the nose.
cards.why: No. That headwind may be a microburst. If you pull power and lower the nose, you are nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

cards.s: A single microburst seldom lasts more than 15 minutes after it reaches the ground.
cards.why: Yes. Its winds keep growing for the first 5 minutes, and it seldom lasts longer than 15 minutes [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]].

final_quiz.q: The Chart Supplement lists no pattern altitude for a non-towered airport at 1,450 feet MSL. What should your altimeter read on downwind in your Cessna?
options: 1,000 feet
1,950 feet
2,450 feet
2,950 feet
final_quiz.why: Propeller airplanes fly the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL unless another altitude is published [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]]. Your altimeter shows MSL: 1,450 + 1,000 = 2,450 feet.

final_quiz.q: You arrive from the upwind side of an airport at 600 feet MSL. Pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL, and business jets use the field. Using the preferred entry, at what altitude should you cross midfield?
options: 2,600 feet MSL
1,600 feet MSL
2,100 feet MSL
3,100 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: Normally you cross at least 500 feet above pattern altitude (1,500 feet AGL). If large or turbine aircraft use the airport, it is best to stay at 2,000 feet AGL [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. 600 + 2,000 = 2,600 feet MSL.

final_quiz.q: Look at panel B, the midfield crosswind entry from the upwind side. When should you NOT use it?
options: When you arrive from the upwind side
When the wind is calm
When the airport uses right traffic
When the pattern is busy
final_quiz.why: Panel B enters on a midfield crosswind at pattern altitude, then turns downwind. It should not be used if the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Arriving from the upwind side is exactly when it is used.

final_quiz.q: You take off from Runway 18, which has right traffic, and want to leave the pattern with a turn. What is recommended?
options: Turn 45° left as soon as you reach 300 feet AGL
Past the departure end and at pattern altitude, turn 45° right
Turn crosswind at midfield, then leave from downwind
Past the departure end and at pattern altitude, turn 45° left
final_quiz.why: Go straight out, or turn 45° beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude: left for left traffic, right for right traffic [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.8]].

final_quiz.q: An airport has an operating tower, but its surface area is Class E, not Class D. When must you have two-way radio contact with the tower?
options: Never, because it is Class E
Before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL
Before 10 NM from the airport, at any altitude
Only when you are ready to turn final
final_quiz.why: At an airport with an operating tower in Class E, you must make two-way contact before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]].

final_quiz.q: Which CTAF call follows FAA guidance?
options: "Any traffic in the area, please advise."
"Cessna 4321X, left downwind for the active runway."
"Cessna 4321X is on downwind, number 2 to land."
"Smithville traffic, Cessna 4321X, entering left downwind Runway 27, Smithville."
final_quiz.why: Say the airport name at the start and end, and say the runway number, not "active runway." "Any traffic, please advise" is not a recognized phrase [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.8.1]]. Don't announce your sequence; that is ATC's job [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

final_quiz.q: Over a non-towered airport with Runways 18-36, you see the large end of the wind sock pointing north. Which runway do you plan to land on?
options: Runway 36
Runway 18
Either one: a wind sock shows only gusts
Neither until UNICOM gives you the wind
final_quiz.why: The large end points into the wind, so the wind is from the north [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]]. Runway 36 points north, most nearly into the wind [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]].

final_quiz.q: Your runway has a displaced threshold: white arrows lead to a white bar. Landing in your direction, how may you use the part with the arrows?
options: Touch down on it to get more landing room
You may not use it for anything
Not for landing, but you may use it for your takeoff roll
Only in an emergency
final_quiz.why: The runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction and for landings from the opposite direction, but not for landing in your direction [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]].

final_quiz.q: On downwind in your Cessna, you converge at the same altitude with a tow plane pulling a glider. It is on your left. Who has the right-of-way?
options: You do, because you are on its right
You do, because you are already in the pattern
Whichever one is lower
The tow plane and glider
final_quiz.why: A glider, including its tow plane while towing, has the right-of-way over powered aircraft [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]]. An aircraft towing another also has the right-of-way over other powered aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]].

final_quiz.q: In which setting do most mid-air collisions happen?
options: At night, in cruise at 8,000 feet
On a clear afternoon, below 1,000 feet, near a non-towered airport
In marginal VFR, near a busy Class C airport
At dusk, between two airplanes meeting head-on
final_quiz.why: Most mid-airs happen in daylight and good visibility, between aircraft going the same direction, at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

final_quiz.q: Look at the figure. You will land with a strong headwind on final. Where should you put your base leg?
options: Closer to the runway than normal
Farther from the runway than normal
In the same place as on a calm day
Skip base and fly a long straight-in
final_quiz.why: With a strong wind on final, put base closer to the approach end than normal [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The figure shows the closest base for the strongest wind.

final_quiz.q: Your POH approach speed is 64 knots. The AWOS reports wind 280 at 12 gusting 22. Using the common rule, about what speed do you fly on final?
options: 64 knots
74 knots
69 knots
86 knots
final_quiz.why: The gust factor is 22 - 12 = 10 knots. Add half of it: 64 + 5 = 69 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Always stay within your POH.

final_quiz.q: A large turboprop just lifted off from your runway as you turn final. Where should you plan to touch down?
options: Beyond the point where it lifted off
Well before the point where it lifted off
Right where it lifted off
Anywhere: a departing airplane leaves no wake
final_quiz.why: Its wake starts at rotation. Note where it rotated and land well before that point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: On final near a thunderstorm, your airspeed suddenly jumps 15 knots and the airplane balloons up. What is the best response?
options: Pull power and lower the nose; the extra speed will last to touchdown
Ignore it; wind shear only affects large airplanes
Slow down more than normal so you can land shorter
Treat it as a possible microburst: expect a tailwind next and be ready to go around
final_quiz.why: A microburst often gives a headwind first, then a tailwind. Cutting power and lowering the nose leaves you nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Be ready to go around at the first sign [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].
